overview: The Khazar confederation linked the Black Sea, Caucasus and lower Volga from the mid-600s to the late 900s. Turkic rulers governed a population with many languages, livelihoods and religions. Its influence depended on trade and diplomacy as well as armies.

periods.title: A steppe power takes shape
periods.summary: Khazar power developed after the breakup of Western Turkic rule.

periods.title: Fortresses and international connections
periods.summary: Don fortresses and correspondence with distant courts illuminate the khaganate's mature period.

periods.title: Loss of central power
periods.summary: Rus and Turkic attacks in the 960s shattered Khazar dominance; sources disagree over the exact sequence.

items.text: Writing around 960, King Joseph described leaving his winter city in spring for vineyards, fields and seasonal work. This is a ruler's account of his own world, but it reminds us that Khazar life included cultivation as well as herding.
Joseph described Jews, Christians and Muslims sharing an urban settlement. His account also mentions enslaved people. Religious variety and commercial connections did not make this an equal society.
Hasdai's letter reports ships carrying fish, skins and other merchandise from Khazaria to Byzantium. River and sea connections helped link northern resources with larger markets.

Joseph credited the earlier ruler Obadiah with supporting synagogues, schools and visiting Jewish scholars. This is evidence of how the court presented its religious learning, not proof that all children attended school.

The British Museum displays iron stirrups and a bridle-bit from near Bielowodsk in the Perm region, dated to the 800s-900s. The possible grave context is uncertain; the objects are associated with the Khazars and their contacts.
Silver sheet decorates the bridle-bit with vines and flowers. The museum connects these motifs with Byzantine and Slavic art. Even horse equipment could carry designs across cultural boundaries.

Sarkel on the lower Don was built with fired brick and had towers, a moat and several internal sectors. These are excavated architectural features, more informative than merely calling the fortress powerful.

At nearby Semikarakorsk, builders combined mud-brick defenses with fired-brick structures in the citadel. The different materials show local construction choices; fired brick was already used there before the Byzantine mission associated with Sarkel.

Workshops adjoined walls at Semikarakorsk and the Tsimliansk Right-bank fortress. These places supported work and administration as well as soldiers. Archaeologist Valery Flyorov warns that the biggest wall circuit need not have been the most defensible.

The Schechter letter credits a woman named Serah with encouraging a ruler's turn toward Judaism. It is a religious story preserved in a later copy, not a contemporary diary; nevertheless, its author gives a woman an active role in the court's remembered history.

The same letter describes a marriage between Joseph and an Alan king's daughter after conflict between their fathers. Its narrative presents marriage as a way of making political peace, rather than a model for all households.

A small Hebrew sample is בארץ קזריא, meaning “in the land of Khazaria.” It appears in the Schechter letter, recto left, line 7. The surviving Cambridge manuscript is a later copy of a text about tenth-century Khazaria, not the ruler's original handwriting.

The famous Kyivan letter should not simply be called Khazar handwriting. A 2026 re-examination finds a mainly Slavic setting and treats a Khazar connection as possible rather than established. Different Hebrew documents need their own histories.

ending.text: Rus and Turkic attacks broke Khazar power during the 960s. The traditional date 965 and Ibn Hawqal's account dated 968-969 cannot be neatly combined into one certain fall day. Refugees returned and communities continued; the map's 1100 endpoint is not an imperial lifetime.
